_national.labelling: Federal rules (TTB, 27 CFR Part 4). Appellation: "American", a state or a county needs 75% from that place (two or three contiguous states or counties: 100%, percentages shown); an AVA needs 85% and the wine must be fully finished in the state (or one of the states) containing the AVA. Varietal: 75% of the named variety, all of it from the labelled appellation (Vitis labrusca varieties 51% with a "contains not less than 51%" statement); two or more varieties may be named only if they make 100%, with percentages shown. Vintage: 95% with an AVA, 85% with other appellations, and an appellation is then mandatory. "Estate Bottled": AVA on the label, winery inside it, all grapes grown on land it owns or controls (lease of at least 3 years) in that AVA, and crushing to bottling in one continuous process on its premises; no other term may imply grower bottling. A vineyard name needs 95% from that vineyard. A brand name of viticultural significance requires the wine to qualify for that place (pre-1986 brands grandfathered).
_national.min_alcohol: Part 4 covers wine of 7 to 24% abv. Table (light) wine up to 14%, dessert wine over 14 to 24%. Stated alcohol tolerance: plus or minus 1.5 points up to 14%, 1 point above 14%, and the statement may not cross the 14% tax-class line.
_national.styles: Sparkling wine may be called "champagne" only with an appellation of origin and as a grandfathered semi-generic name; tank wine must add "bulk process", "charmat method" or similar.
_national.other: About 280 AVAs are listed in 27 CFR Part 9 (October 2026); an AVA is a delimited grape-growing area with no rules on varieties, yields or methods. Semi-generic names (Angelica, Burgundy, Claret, Chablis, Champagne, Chianti, Malaga, Marsala, Madeira, Moselle, Port, Rhine Wine or Hock, Sauterne, Haut Sauterne, Sherry, Tokay) are usable on US wine only with a true appellation of origin and only by brands holding a label approval issued before 10 March 2006. Meritage is not a legal category but a trademark licensed by the Meritage Alliance: red from at least two of Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Cabernet Franc, Malbec, Petit Verdot, St. Macaire, Gros Verdot and Carmenere, white from at least two of Sauvignon Blanc, Semillon and Muscadelle, no variety above 90%. Terms such as Reserve or Old Vine have no federal definition.

region-us-california.labelling: "California" or any California county or AVA: 100% California grapes (state rule, 17 CCR 17015), wine fully produced and finished in California. Conjunctive and county-name statutes: Napa (B&P 25240, 25241), Sonoma (25242, 25246), Paso Robles (25244), Lodi (25245). Federal AVA rule (85%) applies within the 100% California floor.
region-us-california.other: AB 1585 (2025-26) would require 100% US grapes for wine labelled "American" or "United States" sold in California, for wine bottled from 1 July 2027; it passed the Assembly 67-0 in May 2026, but its Senate committee hearing was cancelled at the author's request on 23 June 2026, so it is not law (status checked October 2026).

region-us-oregon.labelling: Oregon rules (OAR 845-010-0905 to 0930, labels from November 2007) apply to all vinifera and hybrid wine produced or bottled in Oregon and to any wine naming Oregon or an Oregon AVA. Variety: 90% of the named variety, except 75% for Cabernet Franc, Cabernet Sauvignon, Carmenere, Durif (Petite Sirah), Grenache, Malbec, Marsanne, Merlot, Mourvedre, Petit Verdot, Roussanne, Sangiovese, Sauvignon Blanc, Semillon, Syrah, Tannat, Tempranillo, Zinfandel. Origin: "Oregon", an Oregon county or an AVA wholly in Oregon requires 100% Oregon grapes and 95% from the named appellation. Semi-generic names banned (narrow "Claret" exception for 2004-2006 label approvals).
region-us-oregon.other: Cross-border AVAs (Columbia Valley, Columbia Gorge, Walla Walla Valley, Snake River Valley): grapes 100% from Oregon and the adjoining state, and the AVA share must meet the lower of 95% or the adjoining state's minimum.

region-us-sonoma-county.labelling: Any AVA lying entirely within Sonoma County (e.g. Russian River Valley, Sonoma Coast, Dry Creek Valley, Alexander Valley) must also show "Sonoma County" (at least 2 mm on bottles over 187 ml) for wines bottled from 1 January 2014 (B&P 25246). The word "Sonoma" in any brand, label or advertising requires the wine to qualify for Sonoma County or an AVA entirely within it and to state it (B&P 25242). 85% AVA rule, 100% California grapes.

region-us-washington.labelling: Washington (RCW 66.28.110, grapes harvested from 2010): if "Washington" is claimed or implied, 95% of the grapes must be from Washington; with "Washington" plus a cross-border AVA, 95% from that AVA or Washington. Otherwise the federal rules apply (AVA 85%, varietal 75%).

us-columbia-gorge.labelling: Cross-border AVA (Washington and Oregon). Federal: 85% from the AVA, wine finished in Washington or Oregon. Washington: if "Washington" also appears, 95% from the AVA or Washington (RCW 66.28.110). Oregon side: grapes 100% from Oregon and Washington, and the AVA share must meet the lower of 95% or the Washington minimum (OAR 845-010-0920(3)); Oregon's 90% varietal rule applies to wine made or bottled in Oregon.

us-lodi.labelling: Wines from any of the seven AVAs lying entirely within Lodi (Mokelumne River, Clements Hills, Jahant and others) must also show "Lodi" (type at most 1 mm smaller than the sub-AVA, at least 2 mm on bottles over 187 ml), for wines bottled from 1 January 2009 (B&P 25245). 85% AVA rule, 100% California grapes.

us-los-carneros.labelling: AVA straddling Napa and Sonoma counties; "Los Carneros" and "Carneros" are both protected names of viticultural significance (27 CFR 9.32). As it is not wholly within either county, the Napa Valley (B&P 25240) and Sonoma County (25246) conjunctive rules do not apply. 85% AVA rule, 100% California grapes.

us-napa-valley.labelling: Federal: 85% from the Napa Valley AVA (75% for "Napa County"). California: 100% California grapes. Conjunctive labelling (B&P 25240): any AVA lying entirely within Napa County (e.g. Oakville, Rutherford, Stags Leap District, Howell Mountain) must also show "Napa Valley" on the label, in type at most 1 mm smaller than the sub-AVA name and at least 2 mm high on bottles over 187 ml, for wines bottled from 1 January 1990. B&P 25241: "Napa" or any Napa AVA name in a brand, label or advertising requires the wine to qualify for the Napa County appellation and to state Napa County or an AVA within it.
us-napa-valley.other: Napa Valley AVA (27 CFR 9.23, January 1981) follows the Napa County line except in the east, where the boundary runs along Putah Creek and the western and southern shores of Lake Berryessa.

us-the-rocks-district-of-milton-freewate.labelling: Lies wholly in Oregon (within Walla Walla Valley), so the full Oregon rules apply: 100% Oregon grapes, 95% from the AVA, 90% varietal (75% for the listed exceptions such as Syrah).

us-walla-walla-valley.labelling: Cross-border AVA (Washington and Oregon), nested in Columbia Valley. Federal: 85% from the AVA, wine finished in Washington or Oregon. Washington: if "Washington" also appears, 95% from the AVA or Washington (RCW 66.28.110). Oregon side: grapes 100% from Oregon and Washington, and the AVA share must meet the lower of 95% or the Washington minimum (OAR 845-010-0920(3)); Oregon's 90% varietal rule applies to wine made or bottled in Oregon.

us-willamette-valley.labelling: Oregon rules (OAR 845-010-0905 to 0930, labels from November 2007) apply to all vinifera and hybrid wine produced or bottled in Oregon and to any wine naming Oregon or an Oregon AVA. Variety: 90% of the named variety, except 75% for Cabernet Franc, Cabernet Sauvignon, Carmenere, Durif (Petite Sirah), Grenache, Malbec, Marsanne, Merlot, Mourvedre, Petit Verdot, Roussanne, Sangiovese, Sauvignon Blanc, Semillon, Syrah, Tannat, Tempranillo, Zinfandel.
